title: Monitor choices for each route permitted both ozone slope signs in four US bird samples in 2005-2019
abstract: We tested whether local ozone monitor choices can change the sign of a weather-adjusted bird richness slope. We used 1,599 paired survey windows on 247 US routes in 2005-2019. Each route used either the nearest or second-nearest available site in all its years within a sample. Exact residual cross-product ranges permit both slope signs in all four East and West, early and late samples. From the all-nearest rule, the fewest route changes needed to reverse the sign were 3, 4, 2 and 6. The two uniform rules agree in sign in three samples. All planned checks also permit both signs, including routes with a stable site pair. These are deliberate worst cases in fixed records, not confidence intervals or causal effects. Choices use bird outcomes, and neither site measures the true bird dose. Selected routes, shared sites, missing days, detection and the fixed model limit inference. The package gives a short proof, attainable assignments, code, site-day evidence, source hashes and independent numerical checks.

display.caption: Sharp mean adjusted cross-product endpoints over all route-specific choices of monitor rank in each sample. Markers show all-nearest and all-second rules. The right panel gives the fewest route changes from all-nearest for each slope sign. Every chosen route uses the same rank in all its retained years within a sample. These are fixed-record sensitivity ranges, not confidence intervals. They use outcomes to find worst cases.
